tldr: Based on the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B video foundation model, the authors built a real-time interactive world model controlled by camera trajectories and a 64-dimensional continuous action stream. It can be trained on just two NVIDIA L20 GPUs and achieves real-time video streaming generation at 24 fps on a single L20.
hero_caption: A collection of diverse video frames generated by Astronex-World 1.0. In addition to text-to-video (T2V) and image-to-video (I2V), it supports persistent streaming generation with interactive camera/action control and dynamic event insertion during rollouts.
overview:
In robotics and autonomous driving research, expectations are rapidly growing for "world models" that can predict future visual observations in real time according to agent actions and camera motion. However, converting existing video diffusion models into interactive world models faces three major barriers. First, high-quality video diffusion models rely on bidirectional attention that looks into the future, making them difficult to convert directly into causal sequential generation that only uses past information. Second, text instructions alone cannot precisely control robots; frame-aligned camera geometry and continuous action inputs must be integrated. Third, continuing to generate frames autoregressively causes errors to accumulate, leading to color drift and structural collapse.

The authors tackled these challenges by developing "Astronex-World 1.0," built on the open 5B-parameter video model "Wan2.2-TI2V-5B," integrating both bidirectional and causal model variants. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are injected directly into each layer via PRoPE (Projective Rotary Position Embedding), while all Transformer layers are modulated by a 64-dimensional continuous action vector and an embodiment identifier (ID). Furthermore, the authors proposed block-causal attention that divides video into 4-frame blocks and caches past Key-Value (KV) states, an attention sink that permanently preserves the first 4 frames, and an elaborate five-stage training pipeline.

Remarkably, all five training stages can be completed on just two workstation-grade NVIDIA L20 (48 GB) GPUs. Scoring 70.0 on the WBench Full 289 benchmark, it not only surpassed YUME 1.5 (68.9)—which was post-trained from the same 5B prior on NVIDIA A100 GPUs—but also outperformed large models in the 13.6B–14B class. Moreover, it achieves real-time persistent streaming at 24 fps (832x480 resolution) on a single L20 GPU, and standard post-training interfaces for robotics and autonomous driving are reserved out of the box.
contributions: Built both a bidirectional model serving as a high-quality teacher and a causal model capable of real-time sequential generation, based on a 5B-parameter video foundation model.

Designed a unified interface that injects precise camera intrinsics and extrinsics via PRoPE and modulates all Transformer layers using a 64-dimensional continuous action stream and embodiment identifiers.

Established an efficient 5-stage training recipe (bidirectional control adaptation, block-causal conversion, online UniPC distillation, domain-mixed SFT, and asymmetric DMD) that runs entirely on just two NVIDIA L20 GPUs.
Demonstrated real-time streaming generation of 832x480 video at 24 fps on a single L20 GPU, achieving a score of 70.0 on WBench Full and outperforming larger 13.6B–14B models.

sections.heading: Why are interactive world models hard, and what does this work aim for?
sections.summary: When converting large pretrained video models into interactive world models, three key tensions emerge: causality, continuous action control, and long-horizon drift. Built on Wan2.2-5B, Astronex-World resolves these challenges on low-cost hardware by providing both bidirectional and causal forms with shared control mechanisms.
sections.details:
A world model is a framework that predicts future observations from current observations and actions. Rather than training this from scratch, researchers aim to leverage the pretrained knowledge of large-scale video foundation models.

However, directly turning existing video diffusion models into interactive world models is not straightforward. There are three fundamental tensions:
- **Bidirectional vs. causal tension**: Existing video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) rely on bidirectional attention looking across all frames simultaneously to ensure high visual quality, but interactive simulation strictly requires a causal structure predicting sequentially from past history.
- **Control granularity**: Text prompts alone cannot direct the physical movements of a robot. The model needs to understand time-synchronized camera geometry and continuous action streams.
- **Error accumulation**: When autoregressively feeding generated frames back as input, the model's own generation errors compound in a loop, resulting in motion decay, geometric distortion, color drift, and loss of fine details.

Astronex-World directly tackles these problems based on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B. It offers two model variants: a "bidirectional model" for high-quality batch generation and teacher scoring, and a "causal model" that operates in real time using few-step sampling and KV caching. Camera control is handled by PRoPE (Projective Rotary Position Embedding), action control employs 64-dimensional continuous vectors, and an action output head is reserved for future robotics applications.

sections.heading: How did world models and video diffusion models evolve?
sections.summary: This section traces the evolution from latent world models in RL to diffusion-based simulators, along with causalization techniques for video DiTs. Extending ideas like Causal Forcing and attention sinks, this work constructs its own training pipeline and control interfaces.
sections.details:
### 2.1 World Models
While latent dynamics models like DreamerV3 are learned by reinforcement learning agents for planning, recent works directly generate visual observations (such as Genie, DIAMOND, and GameNGen). This direction has expanded to autonomous driving (GAIA-1/2, Vista, Cosmos) and robotics (UniSim, UniPi). Rather than confining itself to a specific domain, Astronex-World positions itself as a general camera- and action-conditioned video foundation model.

### 2.2 Video Diffusion and DiTs
Replacing the U-Net backbone with a Transformer, DiTs excel at scaling model capacity. The Wan family provides strong open video foundation models. This work adopts the 30-layer DiT and latent representation of Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, adding control capabilities via LoRA and new modules.

### 2.3 Causal Video Generation and Long-term Memory
Because interactive generation can only look at the past, research has explored distilling bidirectional models (CausVid) and conditioning on self-generated history during training (Self Forcing, Diffusion Forcing). In particular, Causal Forcing (CF) and Causal Forcing++ (CF++) address the transition from bidirectional teachers to causal students. Stages II and III of this work build on CF/CF++. Additionally, to mitigate degradation over long rollouts, the authors incorporate the "attention sink" concept by permanently retaining the KV states of the initial few tokens.

### 2.4 & 2.5 Geometry/Action Control and Few-Step Distillation
While some camera control methods use Plücker coordinates, this work adopts PRoPE, which embeds camera intrinsics and extrinsics via projective geometry. Furthermore, applying distribution matching distillation (DMD/DMD2) enables real-time generation in 4 to 8 steps.

sections.heading: What is the overall architecture of Astronex-World?
sections.summary: The system consists of four layers: data, model, training, and inference/evaluation. Built around a 30-block DiT core, it unifies PRoPE camera control, MLP-based 64D action modulation, and streaming inference using block-causal attention and KV caching within a shared geometric framework.
sections.details:
The system is structured into four distinct layers:
- **Data layer**: Time-aligns RGB video, text, initial frames, camera matrices, action vectors, and embodiment identifiers into latent frame tensors.
- **Model layer**: Retains the Wan2.2 30-block DiT backbone, embedding PRoPE into self-attention and action MLPs into every block's modulation layer. An action output head can also be attached when needed.
- **Training layer**: Switches between bidirectional diffusion, autoregressive diffusion, causal consistency distillation, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and score distillation algorithms.
- **Inference and evaluation layer**: Integrates KV cache management, history windows, the UniPC sampler, and evaluation adapters.

The system provides two primary model configurations: a bidirectional model (restore-2200) and a causal model (causal release). The bidirectional model serves for offline high-quality generation and as a teacher score model during distillation. Meanwhile, the causal model generates video in 8-frame blocks at 832x480 resolution, outputting frames in real time on a single L20 GPU by conditioning on a 20-frame local history window and a 4-frame initial attention sink.

captions.F2: Overview of the Astronex-World model and inference pipeline. (a) The 30-block DiT architecture taking initial frames, noisy latents, camera/action conditions, and text as input. (b) Integration of PRoPE and the action modulation MLP inside each block. (c) Block-wise streaming inference pipeline using a 4-frame attention sink and a 20-frame local window.

sections.heading: How were the datasets designed across camera, robotics, and driving domains?
sections.summary: Control2V from minWM was adopted for camera control training, with re-indexed subsets created to reinforce directional motions. The DROID robotics dataset was used for action control, followed by multi-domain adaptation incorporating autonomous driving and physical contact data.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Camera Control Data
Stage I camera adaptation and Stages II–III causalization utilize "Control2V," an open camera-control dataset. Subsets such as "Control2V_backdown" and "Control2V_combined" were re-indexed to reinforce downward and backward trajectories, enhancing responsiveness to all camera directions. Videos are encoded into 48-channel latents using the Wan2.2 VAE.

### 4.2 Physics and Action Data
For training the action branch (Stage I-b), the real-world robot manipulation dataset "DROID" was used. Each sample includes near-static camera matrices alongside 64-dimensional action data and an embodiment ID. Because the camera rarely moves in robot datasets, the camera learning module (PRoPE) was frozen while only the modulation layers were trained, preventing the model from misidentifying camera identity transforms as actions.

For later adaptation (Stages IV and V), a mixed dataset was constructed by combining Control2V with CrossFPS (first-person gaming), DrivingDojo (driving viewpoints), and NVIDIA PhysicalAI (physical contact), teaching the model diverse real-world dynamics.

sections.heading: How does the model integrate camera, action, and event conditioning?
sections.summary: Text-to-video (T2V) and image-to-video (I2V) are unified in a single network, with camera geometry controlled by PRoPE and 64D action modulation. It also supports dynamic event prompt insertion by taking advantage of KV cache reuse during causal rollouts.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Unified T2V and I2V Design
T2V (generating from text) and I2V (generating future frames from a single image) operate with the exact same weights. The only difference is how the latents are initialized. In I2V, the reference image is embedded into the first frame, kept clean at noise level 0, and excluded from the loss calculation. During Stage IV training, reference frames are kept clean (I2V) 70% of the time and noised (T2V) 30% of the time, allowing a single model to support both tasks.

### 5.2 Block-Causal Generation
In the causal model, temporal attention is modified to a lower-triangular block mask. Within the current 4-frame block, tokens interact bidirectionally, but across blocks, attention is strictly unidirectional (causal) toward the past. Once a block is generated, its KV states are cached, removing the need to recompute the past.

### 5.3 Camera and Action Conditioning
- **Camera (PRoPE)**: Projective transformations are computed from frame intrinsics $K$ and extrinsics $E$, and applied to the Query/Key/Value/Output projections in self-attention across all 30 layers. This directly incorporates relative camera geometry into the attention computation.
- **Action modulation**: The 64-dimensional continuous action vector and embodiment identifier pass through a 2-layer MLP and additively modulate each layer (scale, shift, and gate). The final output layer is zero-initialized to preserve base model behavior initially.
- **Action output head**: An inverse dynamics head is also reserved, pooling visual tokens per frame and passing them through LayerNorm and an MLP to output $[B, F, 64]$ action sequences.

### 5.4 Event Prompt Insertion
A major advantage of the causal model is the ability to append a new event $e$ to the text prompt ($p \oplus e$) starting from a specific frame $s$. Blocks prior to frame $s$ remain unchanged in the KV cache. Only blocks from $s$ onward are generated conditioned on the new text while inheriting the prior visual context, enabling natural transitions such as sudden weather changes or appearing obstacles.

### 5.5 Long-Context Retention
Along with a sliding local window (the most recent 20 frames), the first 4 frames of the video are designated as an "attention sink" that is never evicted from the cache. This prevents the model from forgetting the initial scene appearance and subject identity during long rollouts.

captions.F3: Comparison of T2V and I2V processing flows sharing the same DiT backbone. (a) In T2V, all frames start from Gaussian noise and share the same diffusion timestep. (b) In I2V, the first frame is fixed with a clean reference image (timestep 0), and only the remaining frames are denoised.
captions.F4: Mechanism for dynamic event prompt insertion in the causal model. The KV cache before a specified frame $s$ is preserved intact; from frame $s$ onward, the text is re-encoded with the appended prompt, altering events while maintaining past visual context.

sections.heading: How is the 5-stage training recipe run on just two GPUs?
sections.summary: The authors established a 5-stage training procedure that progressively transitions the model from bidirectional control to causal generation, distillation, domain adaptation, and asymmetric DMD distribution matching—all on two NVIDIA L20 (48 GB) GPUs.
sections.details:
The complete training recipe consists of five progressive stages:

### 6.1–6.3 Stage I: Bidirectional Control Adaptation
Starting from Wan2.2 pretrained weights, LoRA and PRoPE are trained using full bidirectional attention across all frames.
- **I-a (Camera)**: Learns camera following on Control2V (checkpoint 2400).
- **I-b (Action)**: Freezes PRoPE and trains the 64D action branch using the DROID dataset.
- **I-c (Camera Restoration)**: Restores camera responsiveness degraded during action training by resuming training on Control2V (producing restore-2200, which serves as the public bidirectional model and subsequent teacher).
- **I-d (Direction Reinforcement)**: Further fine-tunes camera control using combined directional subsets.

### 6.4 Stage II: Block-Causal Conversion via Teacher Forcing
The temporal attention mask is switched to a block lower-triangular structure, training a multi-step autoregressive diffusion model that denoises the current block conditioned on clean past blocks (500 steps).

### 6.5 Stage III: Online UniPC Trajectory Distillation
Using the Stage II model as a teacher, the student model learns the 12-step UniPC sampling trajectory used at inference time. It is distilled using Smooth L1 loss and temporal difference loss to match the teacher's dense 25-step trajectory (20 steps).

### 6.6 Stage IV: Mixed-Domain Causal SFT
Because training on camera-only data tends to yield static subjects, the model is fine-tuned for 540 steps on a mixed dataset including gaming, driving, and robotics data (CrossFPS, DrivingDojo, PhysicalAI). Rolling Forcing, which conditions on self-generated rollout history, is applied with an 80% probability.

### 6.7 Stage V: Asymmetric DMD/DMD2 with Motion-Preserving Loss
Distribution matching distillation (DMD) is applied to push quality in the few-step regime (4–8 steps). The key is "asymmetry": while the generator is causal, the frozen teacher computing real-data distribution scores is the high-quality "bidirectional model (restore-2200)" from Stage I. Additionally, to counteract the "over-staticization" common in DMD where motion freezes, a motion-preserving loss ($L_{\mathrm{motion}}$) was introduced to match adjacent-frame latent differences to real data (checkpoint 1545 is the final release).

captions.F6: Noise schedules and objectives across training stages. (a) Latent corruption via flow matching. (b) Shared frame-wide timesteps in Stage I vs. block-wise timesteps in Stages II–IV. (c) Asymmetric DMD configuration in Stage V with a causal generator, frozen bidirectional real teacher, and online fake critic.

sections.heading: How are streaming inference and objective evaluations set up?
sections.summary: The causal model performs real-time inference at 832x480 resolution and 24 fps on a single L20 using 8-step UniPC. Evaluation uses the comprehensive interactive benchmark WBench (Navi 158 and Full 289) and standard VBench 1.0.
sections.details:
### 7.1 Default Inference Configuration
The released causal model uses an 8-step UniPC sampler with Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG=3.0), generating chunks of 8 latent frames (approximately 32 RGB frames) per block. By reusing the KV cache and conditioning on a 20-frame local history and a 4-frame sink, frames are streamed sequentially as each block finishes without waiting for the full rollout. A single NVIDIA L20 (48 GB) achieves real-time generation at 24 fps.

### 7.2 WBench Evaluation Protocol
WBench is a standard benchmark for evaluating interactive world models, comprising 289 test cases and 1,058 interaction rounds. It features two subsets: "Navi 158," which tests navigation only, and "Full 289," which also includes event editing, subject manipulation, and viewpoint switches. Instead of re-generating per turn, videos are rolled out continuously for up to 35+ seconds. The latest Doubao VLM model is used as the judge.

### 7.3 VBench 1.0
Using the official VBench codebase, 240 text-to-video (T2V) and 118 image-to-video (I2V) samples were evaluated to measure visual quality and temporal consistency objectively.

sections.heading: How does it achieve remarkable cost efficiency and outperform larger models?
sections.summary: Achieving a score of 70.0 on WBench Full, it outperformed not only the 5B YUME 1.5 but also 13.6B–14B models. While it scored exceptionally high in visual quality and consistency, limitations were observed in event interaction and motion dampening.
sections.details:
### 8.1 & 8.2 Benchmark Comparisons
On WBench Full 289, Astronex-World 1.0 achieved an overall score of 70.0 (and 73.5 on Navi 158).
- **Comparison within 5B class**: It outperformed YUME 1.5 (68.9)—which was post-trained on A100 clusters from the same Wan2.2-5B base—by 1.1 points, winning in 4 out of 5 dimensions. It also led the 4B Kairos 3.0 (65.7) by 4.3 points.
- **Comparison with large models (13B–22B)**: It surpassed models with more than twice its parameter count, such as LongCat-Video (13.6B, 69.9) and Helios (14B, 69.7), and came within 0.9 points of the 22B LTX-2.3 (70.9). Notably, while Helios used 64 to 128 H100 GPUs per stage, this work trained on only two L20 GPUs.
- **Sub-dimension scores**: It set the highest Quality score among all models at 78.3 and achieved an outstanding 82.4 in Consistency.

### 8.3–8.6 Qualitative Evaluation and Analysis
Qualitative results show that subject identity and background geometry remain intact even through wide camera pans and forward motion. On the other hand, the Interaction score fell from 63.4 on Navi 158 to 47.6 on Full 289. This drop occurs because the current mechanism relies on simple text prompt appending, which struggles with multiple concurrent events or complex subject actions.

### 8.8 Motion Diagnostics (Detecting Over-staticization)
During development testing on a basketball sequence, DMD distillation boosted visual quality and stability but introduced "over-staticization," damping the dynamic movements of subjects. Although mitigated by the motion-preserving loss, motion amplitude still fell short of the original bidirectional model, representing an area for future improvement.

captions.F9: Consistency evaluation of generated sequences on WBench. Insets show that the texture and morphology of subjects (astronaut and hot-air balloon, red boxes) and the architectural geometry and color of urban canals (blue boxes) are faithfully preserved across long causal rollouts.

sections.heading: What are the limitations of the current model?
sections.summary: Limitations include the inability to control multiple complex events simultaneously, color drift during long rotations, motion damping caused by distillation, and the lack of explicit physical simulation.
sections.details:
The paper candidly highlights the following limitations:
- **Weakness in complex interactions**: While strong at continuous camera and action tracking, controlling multiple timed events or intricate subject gestures via text switching remains limited.
- **Drift in long rollouts**: Although the attention sink significantly delays forgetting, long rollouts featuring sharp U-turns, closed loops, or dark scenes still exhibit gradual darkening or texture hallucination.
- **Motion damping**: Because DMD distillation tends to favor stable, average solutions, dynamic subject movements are more restrained compared to the bidirectional model.
- **Physical fidelity**: Without explicit 3D meshes, depth, or rigid-body collision solvers, visual plausibility is achieved without guaranteed strict physical simulation.

sections.heading: What is planned for the next-generation Astronex-World 2.0?
sections.summary: Future plans include adding a 14B model alongside the 5B scale and eliminating drift through structured memory training with geometric and photometric constraints. The reserved action interfaces will also be applied to real robots and autonomous driving.
sections.details:
For the next generation, "Astronex-World 2.0," the authors plan to maintain the 5B model for low-cost deployment while introducing a 14B model capable of handling more complex physical dynamics.

To tackle long-horizon color drift and loop inconsistency—the core research challenge—the team aims to combine deeper integration of bidirectional priors with causal rollouts, geometric and photometric consistency constraints, and external memory for structured retrieval of past viewpoints. Additionally, they plan to utilize the reserved 64D action input and output heads to connect with real robot joint angles, gripper controls, and vehicle steering/pedals, directly evaluating action planning and downstream task success rates.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Opening new frontiers for world models on modest compute
sections.summary: Astronex-World 1.0 proves that a state-of-the-art interactive world model can be built without massive clusters through clever training recipes and model design, offering a strong foundation for open robotics and autonomous driving research.
sections.details:
The central takeaway of this work is that a top-tier real-time world model can be achieved without massive GPU clusters or ultra-large parameter scales, provided one starts from a strong pretrained video model and applies an elaborate, staged post-training recipe.

Despite being trained on just two NVIDIA L20 GPUs—an accessible setup for standard laboratories—it outperformed 14B models and prior works trained on vast H100 clusters. Featuring real-time streaming generation and open action interfaces, Astronex-World 1.0 provides a practical, highly reproducible, and powerful baseline for future research in robot learning and embodied intelligence.

takeaways: Causalizing video DiTs into world models can be achieved at high quality on modest GPU setups by combining block-wise conversion from a bidirectional teacher, online trajectory distillation, and asymmetric DMD.

Injecting camera intrinsics and extrinsics via PRoPE combined with an attention sink (permanently retaining the initial frames) is highly effective for maintaining long-term geometric and appearance consistency.
Using distillation (DMD) for few-step sampling and higher fidelity carries the side effect of damping dynamics, making explicit countermeasures like a motion-preserving loss essential.
Integrating an inverse dynamics action output head into the architecture from the beginning enables smooth future expansion toward robotics applications alongside real-time visual prediction.
limitations: Event control via text prompt appending cannot precisely handle multiple concurrent time-specified events or complex subject gestures.
Over long causal rollouts, color fading, darkening, and detail hallucination (drift) still occur during sharp turns or in dark scenes.
Distribution matching via DMD tends to suppress the large subject motion amplitudes originally present in the bidirectional base model.
